strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: applying Critic-free, GRPO-style group-based RL to multi-agent LLM systems (MAS), which is timely given the popularity of GRPO/DAPO and growing interest in agentic LLM pipelines.

The proposed backward reward-propagation mechanism and the three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) are conceptually clear and provide a reasonable design space exploring the efficiency/effectiveness trade-off for heterogeneous multi-agent rollout grouping.

Reasonably thorough empirical analysis including training curves, GPU memory/time profiling, per-agent output pattern evolution, intra-group similarity analysis, and a qualitative case study, which together provide some mechanistic insight into why heterogeneous-group advantage estimation works (i.e., convergence toward homogeneous groups).
Detailed appendix with full algorithms and hyperparameters improves reproducibility of the described procedure.
Results consistently show MHGPO variants (esp. FoF/RR) outperforming MAPPO in accuracy/EM/F1 while reducing GPU memory and time, which if robust would be a useful practical contribution.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single 3-agent MASS architecture, single training dataset (HotpotQA) with only cross-dataset (not cross-task/topology) transfer, and a single backbone model (Llama3.1-8B); no ablation on group size G, number of agents, or different MAS topologies, limiting evidence for generality claimed in the contributions and conclusion.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed runs reported for the main results table (Table 1) or efficiency figures (Figure 6), making it hard to assess whether the reported gains over MAPPO are statistically meaningful versus run-to-run noise, especially given RL training instability is a central motivating concern of the paper.

The theoretical justification for why relative advantage estimation over heterogeneous groups (mixing different input prompts within the same GRPO-style normalization) is a valid/unbiased advantage estimator is not rigorously established; the paper offers a post-hoc empirical explanation (heterogeneous groups gradually become homogeneous) rather than a principled analysis, leaving the core algorithmic claim under-justified for early training stages when groups are truly heterogeneous.

Comparison baseline is limited to MAPPO; no comparison to other recent GRPO/DAPO adaptations for multi-agent or long-horizon RL, nor to simpler baselines such as independent per-agent GRPO with proper reward shaping, weakening the claim of being the first/best systematic GOA investigation for MAS.

The reward design (shared reward backpropagation via simple averaging, plus hand-crafted agent-specific format penalties) is fairly specific to this QA/search pipeline and its generalization to other MAS reward structures (e.g., non-linear agent graphs, cyclic interactions) is asserted but not demonstrated.

Writing/organization could be tightened: some notation (e.g., Gk, candidate group G'_k) is introduced without full clarity, and the RR probability schedule (0.7, 0.1, 0.2) appears manually tuned without justification or sensitivity analysis.

Only one epoch of training and relatively small-scale rollout group size (G=4) are used; it's unclear how the method scales with larger group sizes or longer training, which is relevant to the claimed compute-efficiency advantage over PPO.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: extending critic-free, group-based RL (GRPO-style) advantage estimation to multi-agent LLM systems, which currently rely on costly and unstable Critic-based MAPPO training.

The proposed heterogeneous-group reward propagation and three rollout strategies (IS, FoF, RR) are conceptually clear and the paper provides a reasonably detailed algorithmic description (including pseudocode) that aids understanding and potential reproduction.

The empirical comparison against MAPPO shows consistent gains in both task metrics and training efficiency/memory on the tested search-agent pipeline, and the paper includes informative diagnostic analyses (agent behavior evolution, intra-group similarity, case studies) that offer some mechanistic insight into why the method works.
The writing and figures are generally clear, and the paper situates itself reasonably well with respect to prior MARL-for-MAS and GOA literature.
weaknesses: Experimental scope is narrow: a single fixed 3-agent, strictly sequential MASS architecture, a single backbone model (Llama3.1-8B), and training exclusively on HotpotQA, while the paper repeatedly claims general applicability to arbitrary MAS; this generality is asserted but never tested (e.g., no branching agent topologies, no other backbone sizes/families).

No variance/seed reporting: all reported numbers (Table 1, Figures 5/6/8/9/11) appear to come from single runs, despite well-documented instability of RL training for LLMs; without repeated trials or confidence intervals, claims of MHGPO's superior stability and performance are not statistically substantiated.

Missing a critical ablation: a direct comparison to naive single-agent GRPO/DAPO applied independently to each agent (without the heterogeneous-group or reward-propagation machinery) would isolate the contribution of the proposed heterogeneous grouping and backward reward propagation; without it, it is unclear how much of the improvement over MAPPO stems from being critic-free per se versus the specific heterogeneous-group design.

The reward aggregation function Aggr(·) is instantiated only as simple averaging with no justification or sensitivity analysis, and in the tested strictly linear 3-agent chain each agent has only a single successor, making the aggregation trivial; the more general/branching case that would stress-test this design choice is never evaluated.

The Round-Robin fork probabilities (0.7, 0.1, 0.2) are fixed without ablation or principled derivation, and are likely dataset/architecture-specific, raising reproducibility and generalizability concerns.

The efficiency comparison against MAPPO uses a critic identical in size to the actor, which is a somewhat unfavorable/uncommon configuration for PPO baselines; a more standard smaller critic or head-only critic baseline is not explored, potentially inflating the apparent efficiency gains.

The paper's claim of being the 'first systematic investigation of GOAs applied to MASs' is in tension with the cited concurrent work MARFT (Liao et al., 2025b), which appears to already propose an RL framework for MAS; the differentiation from this closely related work is not clearly articulated.

The explanatory discussion in Section 'Why does heterogeneous-group-based policy optimization work?' (groups becoming homogeneous over training) is an interesting but largely correlational/post-hoc observation, not a rigorously validated causal account.

Overall, the contribution is an incremental, engineering-oriented combination of known techniques (GRPO-style relative advantage estimation + MAPPO-style parameter sharing + heuristic reward backpropagation), and the evidence provided, while suggestive, does not yet meet the bar of rigor (multiple seeds, broader task/model diversity, key ablations) expected for a main-conference contribution.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: eliminating the critic network for MARL fine-tuning of LLM-based multi-agent systems, which is a real pain point (instability, memory overhead) with MAPPO-style approaches.

The proposed MHGPO framework, including the backward reward-propagation mechanism and the notion of heterogeneous vs. homogeneous group advantage estimation, is a reasonably novel extension of GRPO/DAPO-style group-relative advantage estimation to the multi-agent setting.

The three rollout sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) are clearly motivated and explore a sensible efficiency/effectiveness trade-off space, with RR representing a nontrivial engineering contribution (batch-level regrouping).

Empirical evaluation is fairly comprehensive: main results across three QA benchmarks (in- and out-of-domain), training dynamics (validation curves, reward curves, format-penalty curves), compute/memory profiling, output-pattern analysis, intra-group similarity analysis, and a qualitative case study.
Efficiency gains are clearly and convincingly demonstrated (lower GPU memory and comparable/lower wall-clock time vs. MAPPO), which is a concrete, reproducible practical benefit.

The paper is transparent about implementation details (prompts, hyperparameters, reward design, and detailed pseudocode for all three sampling algorithms), aiding reproducibility despite reliance on an internal Wikipedia/contriever retrieval setup.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single backbone (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct) and a single MAS architecture (the three-agent search system); despite claims of general applicability to MAS, no evidence is given beyond this one instantiation, so generalization claims are unsupported.

The theoretical justification for computing relative advantage over 'heterogeneous' groups (rollouts from different agents/inputs) is thin. Unlike standard GRPO, where the group baseline is a valid Monte Carlo estimate of the value for a shared input, here group members share only an identifier but not an input distribution; the paper's explanation (heterogeneous groups 'naturally evolve' into homogeneous ones) is post hoc and correlational rather than a rigorous bias/variance analysis of the advantage estimator.

No statistical significance or variance across seeds is reported; all results (Table 1, Figures 5casino) appear to be single runs, which is a concern given RL training is known to be high-variance, especially for a paper making comparative claims against MAPPO.

Results are not fully consistent with the paper's narrative: on MuSiQue, MHGPO-RR underperforms MAPPO on Accuracy and EM despite being highlighted as the best/most efficient variant; this inconsistency is not discussed.

Key hyperparameters (e.g., RR's per-agent fork probabilities (0.7, 0.1, 0.2), group size G=4) are fixed without ablation, so sensitivity of MHGPO's performance/efficiency trade-off to these choices is unclear.

The reward design (F1-based shared reward plus hand-crafted agent-specific format penalties) is fairly task-specific engineering; it is unclear how much of the observed gains stem from this reward shaping versus the core algorithmic contribution.

Only one MARL baseline (MAPPO) is compared; other relevant baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., HAPPO, MARFT) or naive single-agent GRPO applied per-agent are not empirically compared, limiting the strength of the comparative claims.
No code/artifact release is mentioned, and the retrieval pipeline (Wikipedia dump + contriever) relies on external setup that may hinder exact reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and timely gap: extending critic-free, group-relative RL (GRPO-style) methods to multi-agent, multi-context search systems, where naive single-context GRPO does not directly apply due to disjoint agent contexts.

The proposed backward reward propagation plus heterogeneous-group advantage estimation is a sensible and clearly explained mechanism for handling indirect inter-agent dependencies and implicit cross-trajectory correlations.

Thorough empirical evaluation: training dynamics (reward/F1 curves), compute/memory cost comparisons against MAPPO, per-agent behavior tracking (sub-query counts, doc selection, answer length), and several targeted ablations (role-wise freezing/training, reward-aggregation operator, sparse vs. composite reward, group size).

Consistent and fairly large empirical gains over MAPPO and single-context RAG-RL baselines (Search-o1, R1-Searcher) on in-domain HotpotQA and out-of-domain 2WikiMultihopQA/MuSiQue, together with lower GPU memory and comparable/lower wall-clock cost.

An explicit, if idealized, theoretical bridge (Appendix D) connecting MHGPO to single-context GRPO under a context-sufficiency assumption, which helps interpret why and when the heterogeneous-group approach should work.
Practically useful exploration of sampling-strategy trade-offs (IS/FoF/RR/FoF-os), giving practitioners concrete guidance on efficiency-vs-performance trade-offs.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single fixed 3-agent pipeline (Rewriter→Reranker→Answerer) and a single 8B backbone; generalization to different team sizes, non-linear/branching agent topologies, or larger models is untested, despite the paper's framing as a general MAS/MASS method (explicitly acknowledged as a limitation).
Task scope is narrow (multi-hop QA with static retrieval only); no evidence for open-ended agentic search, planning, or tool-heavy settings the introduction motivates the work with.

The main results table (Table 1), which drives the central performance claims, reports single-run numbers with no variance/error bars or significance testing, whereas variance is only shown in secondary ablation tables (3 seeds); this weakens confidence in the magnitude of reported gains over strong baselines like MAPPO.

Reward design relies on hand-crafted, agent-specific format penalties (query count, doc redundancy, answer length) that require non-trivial task-specific engineering, somewhat undercutting the 'automated end-to-end' motivation contrasted with prompt engineering/SFT in the introduction.

The formal single-context equivalence (Appendix D) rests on a strong context-sufficiency assumption the authors admit is rarely satisfied in practice, so its contribution is mainly illustrative/conceptual rather than a rigorous guarantee for the empirically used relaxed regime.

Limited discussion of comparability/fairness with MAPPO tuning (e.g., critic architecture, hyperparameter search depth) and no comparison to other recent multi-agent RL fine-tuning methods (e.g., MARFT, cited but not empirically compared), leaving open whether gains are due to the core algorithmic idea or implementation/tuning differences.

The claim that intra-group homogenization is 'not entropy collapse' is only weakly supported (correlation with improved F1) rather than directly tested, leaving open questions about long-term training stability/diversity loss.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: extending critic-free, group-based RL (GRPO-style) methods to multi-context, multi-agent LLM pipelines, where naive within-prompt grouping is not directly applicable.

The proposed backward reward propagation plus heterogeneous-group advantage estimation is a reasonably clear and implementable mechanism, and the three sampling strategies (IS/FoF/RR, plus FoF with oversampling) offer a sensible exploration of the efficiency-effectiveness tradeoff space.

Reasonably thorough empirical analysis: training dynamics, GPU memory/time comparisons against MAPPO, role-wise ablations (freezing/training single agents), reward-aggregation-operator ablations, and a sparse-reward stress test (Table 4) that collectively support the claim that MHGPO captures cross-agent coordination rather than merely improving agents independently.
Reports consistent gains over an unoptimized MAS and over MAPPO on in-domain and two OOD multi-hop QA datasets, with lower reported memory/time cost than the critic-based baseline.
weaknesses: Table 1 contains what appear to be implausible baseline numbers: PPO/GRPO (single-context RL baselines) show EM scores near 0-2% while their Accuracy/F1 are 20-30%, an enormous and unexplained gap that strongly suggests an evaluation or implementation bug (e.g., in EM/answer-format normalization) rather than a genuine capability gap; this undermines confidence in the fairness/correctness of the comparative results throughout the table.

The most directly comparable prior work, MARFT (Liao et al. 2025a/b), which is explicitly about multi-agent RL fine-tuning for LLM systems, is discussed in related work but never used as an experimental baseline; MAPPO is the only MARL baseline compared, which is a narrow basis for the paper's central efficiency/stability claims.

The 'theoretical bridge' to single-context GRPO (Appendix D) rests on an idealized context-sufficiency assumption (A3) that the paper itself repeatedly acknowledges does not hold in realistic MAS settings; as presented, this equivalence proof is close to a restatement of the algorithm's construction (broadcasting the same reward to tokens under matched groupings trivially reproduces GRPO) rather than a substantive theoretical result, and its practical relevance to the 'relaxed regime' claims is asserted rather than analyzed (no variance/stability bound is derived, as the paper itself notes).

Experiments are confined to a single 8B backbone, a single fixed 3-agent linear pipeline (Rewriter→Reranker→Answerer), and QA-only tasks with static retrieval; scalability to larger models, different topologies, or more complex tool-use/planning settings is entirely untested, limiting the evidence for the claimed general applicability to broader MAS.

Reward design still requires hand-crafted per-agent format penalties (agent-specific reward functions), which partially undercuts the 'automated end-to-end' motivation given in the introduction as a key advantage over prompt engineering/SFT.

Efficiency comparisons (Fig. 6) and the FoF(os) variant's extra rollout cost are not clearly normalized against each other in the main results table, making the claimed 'performance-efficiency trade-off' harder to assess quantitatively across variants.
Supporting qualitative evidence (Fig. 9 case study) is a single anecdotal example, which is only illustrative and not substantive evidence for the mechanism claims made in Section 4.3.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and genuinely non-trivial problem: extending critic-free, group-relative policy optimization (GRPO-style) from single-context reasoning to multi-agent, multi-context pipelines, where rollouts from different agents have disjoint local contexts.

The proposed backward reward propagation plus heterogeneous-group advantage estimation is a sensible and reasonably novel mechanism for attributing global (terminal) reward to upstream agents without a critic.

Thorough exploration of the design space via three rollout-sampling strategies (IS, FoF, RR) plus an over-sampling variant, with a clear articulation of their sample-efficiency vs. optimization-quality trade-offs, backed by both training dynamics (Fig. 5) and resource-cost measurements (Fig. 6).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical study: comparisons against MAPPO, PPO, GRPO, single-context RAG-RL baselines (Search-o1, R1-Searcher), plus in-domain and two OOD multi-hop QA datasets, along with ablations on role-wise training (Table 2), reward-aggregation operator choice (Table 3), and sparse vs. composite reward regimes (Table 4).
Good efficiency analysis showing substantially lower GPU memory and comparable/lower wall-clock cost relative to MAPPO, which is a practically relevant claim given the motivation of the paper.

The formal bridge to single-context GRPO under an idealized context-sufficiency assumption (Appendix D) is a thoughtful theoretical anchor, and the paper is appropriately careful in framing it as a conceptual rather than operational equivalence.

Interpretable behavioral analyses (agent output length/format convergence, intra-group similarity, case study) support the narrative that MHGPO induces coordinated, stable multi-agent behavior rather than just improving isolated agents.
weaknesses: Main results (Table 1) are reported without variance/error bars or multiple seeds, unlike the ablation tables (2-4, 6) which do report seed variance; this weakens confidence in the headline comparisons, especially for close margins between MHGPO variants and MAPPO on OOD datasets.

Some baseline numbers appear anomalous and are not well explained: PPO/GRPO (direct RL-tuned LLMs) show extremely low EM (e.g., 0.500-2.600) despite comparatively higher Accuracy/F1, which is an unusual pattern that could reflect answer-formatting/normalization issues in the baseline setup rather than a genuine capability gap; more discussion or verification is needed.

Experimental scope is narrow: a single 8B backbone (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct), a single fixed 3-agent linear pipeline (Rewriter→Reranker→Answerer), and one task family (multi-hop QA with static retrieval). Claims of general applicability to "broader MASs" and arbitrary n are asserted but not empirically tested, so generalizability remains unverified.

The MAPPO baseline's competitiveness/instability depends heavily on critic implementation and tuning details, which are only briefly described (critic shares actor architecture, single set of hyperparameters); without more tuning transparency it is hard to rule out that MAPPO's reported instability partly reflects suboptimal critic configuration rather than an inherent limitation of critic-based MARL.

The agent-specific reward design (format penalties) is somewhat hand-crafted and task-specific (e.g., penalizing >4 sub-queries, response length thresholds), and while ablated in the composite-vs-final-only setting, its sensitivity/generality across other MAS designs is not explored.

The theoretical equivalence result (Appendix D) relies on a strong context-sufficiency assumption (A3) that the paper itself acknowledges is generally violated in practice; while framed honestly as an idealized anchor, it does not by itself provide guarantees (e.g., variance bounds) for the more realistic regime the method is designed for, and this gap is explicitly left to future work.

No direct empirical comparison against other recently proposed MARL fine-tuning frameworks explicitly cited as related work (e.g., MARFT), which would help contextualize how much of the improvement is attributable to the specific heterogeneous-grouping design versus general critic-free MARL adaptation.
